hints: Focus on symmetry rather than just bond polarity, as polar bonds can cancel out completely in a symmetrical shape.
Recall the shapes: boron trifluoride is trigonal planar, methane is tetrahedral, and phosphorus pentafluoride is trigonal bipyramidal.
Check if the bond dipoles point equally in all directions in each case, so they add to zero and leave no overall dipole.
walkthrough:
**Recall when dipoles cancel**

A molecule can have polar bonds but still have zero overall dipole if it is perfectly symmetrical.

Think of it as equal pulls in opposite directions:
$$\text{vector sum of bond dipoles} = 0$$

**Check boron trifluoride, $\text{BF}_3$**

Boron has 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so it is trigonal planar with $120^{\circ}$ angles.

The three $\text{B-F}$ bonds are polar, but they are spaced equally and cancel, so no overall dipole.

**Check methane, $\text{CH}_4$**

Carbon has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so it is tetrahedral and perfectly symmetrical.

The four $\text{C-H}$ bond dipoles are arranged equally in space and cancel, so no overall dipole.

**Check phosphorus pentafluoride, $\text{PF}_5$**

Phosphorus has 5 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so it is trigonal bipyramidal and also symmetrical.

The five $\text{P-F}$ bonds are polar, but the axial dipoles cancel each other and the three equatorial dipoles cancel each other, so no overall dipole.

**Conclude the combination**

Since 1, 2 and 3 all have symmetrical shapes that cancel their polar bond dipoles, all three have no overall dipole moment.

options.A: Correct. All three are symmetrical with no lone pairs on the central atom. $\text{BF}_3$ is trigonal planar, $\text{CH}_4$ is tetrahedral, and $\text{PF}_5$ is trigonal bipyramidal, so in each case the polar bond dipoles cancel to zero.
options.B: Incorrect. This suggests only 1 and 2 have no dipole. It wrongly leaves out phosphorus pentafluoride. Students sometimes forget the trigonal bipyramidal shape is also symmetrical and think 5 bonds cannot cancel.
options.C: Incorrect. This suggests only 2 and 3 have no dipole. It wrongly leaves out boron trifluoride. Students sometimes confuse trigonal planar $\text{BF}_3$ with pyramidal shapes like ammonia that do have a dipole.
options.D: Incorrect. This suggests only 1 has no dipole. It wrongly leaves out methane and phosphorus pentafluoride. This comes from thinking only flat 2D symmetry can cancel, while tetrahedral and bipyramidal 3D symmetry also cancels perfectly.
